The price paid by the assignee to the assignor is not liable to GST, although GIDC's own transfer charges remain taxable. The notices and orders were quashed; the Supreme Court declined to interfere.
cases.effect: Selling an industrial plot held on a long lease, by assigning the lease with or without the building, is outside GST; the development authority's transfer fee is still taxable. The authority's original grant of the lease remains a taxable supply of services (see Builders Association of Navi Mumbai; entry 41 of Notification 12/2017-CT(Rate) exempts the upfront premium for qualifying industrial plots). The ruling is about an outright assignment — a sub-lease, or a fresh lease for rent, is still a supply.

cases.name: Indian Medical Association, Kerala State Branch v. Union of India
cases.citation: 2025:KER:30517, W.A. No. 1659 of 2024 with W.A. Nos. 1487 of 2024 and 468 of 2025, decided 11-04-2025 (Dr A.K. Jayasankaran Nambiar and Easwaran S. JJ.) — from the single judge's judgment of 23-07-2024; the Union's special leave petitions (C) Nos. 18349–18350 of 2025 are pending in the Supreme Court
cases.facts: The Kerala branch of the IMA runs schemes and facilities for its member doctors and faced DGGI action to recover GST on them. It challenged section 7(1)(aa) and section 2(17)(e), inserted by the Finance Act 2021 with effect from 1 July 2017 to tax an association's activities for its members by deeming the two to be separate persons. A single judge held the retrospective operation invalid; both sides appealed.
cases.issue: Can Parliament tax transactions between an association and its own members — overriding the principle of mutuality — by deeming them to be separate persons?
cases.held: No. 'Supply' and 'service', as the Constitution uses them in Articles 246A and 366(12A), need two persons, and in Calcutta Club the Supreme Court held that mutuality survived the 46th Amendment; a statutory deeming fiction cannot enlarge those constitutional concepts without a constitutional amendment. Sections 2(17)(e) and 7(1)(aa), with the Explanation, in the CGST Act and the Kerala GST Act were declared unconstitutional and void for want of legislative competence. The Bench also agreed that their retrospective operation was unfair and illegal.
cases.effect: Clubs, associations and resident welfare associations rely on it for what they provide to members. It binds within Kerala; elsewhere the provisions have not been struck down, and the Union's appeal is pending in the Supreme Court. Supplies to non-members are taxable either way — keep them separately recorded.

cases.name: K.C. Overseas Education Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India
cases.citation: Bombay High Court (Nagpur Bench), Writ Petition Nos. 3914 and 4069 of 2024, decided 03-03-2025 (Avinash G. Gharote and Abhay J. Mantri JJ.); the Union's special leave petitions (C) Nos. 21104–21105 of 2025 dismissed on 25-08-2025
cases.facts: An education consultant in Nagpur recruits Indian students for foreign universities under agreements with the universities, which pay it commission in foreign currency. It paid GST on the commission and sought a refund, treating the service as an export; the refund was refused on the ground that it was an intermediary with its place of supply in India, and the appellate authority agreed on 07-03-2024.
cases.issue: Is a consultant engaged and paid by foreign universities to recruit students an intermediary, or an exporter of services?
cases.held: An exporter. Reading the definition of export of services in section 2(6) as a whole — with 'recipient' (the person liable to pay the consideration, section 2(93) of the CGST Act), section 13(2) and the definition of intermediary in section 2(13) — and following the Delhi High Court in Ernst & Young, which considered Circular 159/15/2021, the consultant was not an intermediary. CESTAT had already held in the consultant's own service tax case that it served the universities that paid it, not the students, and the definition of intermediary is the same in both regimes. The appellate order was quashed and the refund of GST allowed, subject to receipt of the consideration in foreign currency. The Supreme Court dismissed the department's petitions in view of its judgment of 06-05-2025 in Commissioner of Service Tax v. Vodafone India Ltd.
cases.effect: For supplies up to 29 March 2026 — when section 13(8)(b) still placed intermediary services in India — a supplier engaged and paid by a foreign principal for its own service is not an intermediary merely because it deals with people in India on the principal's behalf. Section 13(8)(b) was omitted from 30 March 2026, so the question now matters for earlier periods and pending refund claims.

cases.name: Patson Papers Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India
cases.citation: Gujarat High Court, R/Special Civil Application No. 26250 of 2022 with connected petitions (2025); the Union's special leave petition (Diary No. 49578 of 2025) dismissed by the Supreme Court in October 2025
cases.facts: Manufacturers bought coal, paying compensation cess on it, and exported finished goods — which attract no cess — on payment of IGST. Their claims for refund of the unutilised cess credit were rejected on the strength of Circulars 45/19/2018 and 125/44/2019 (no refund of cess credit where exports are made on payment of IGST) and the proviso to section 11(2) of the Compensation Cess Act, which confines cess credit to paying cess.
cases.issue: Can an exporter that pays IGST on exported goods not liable to cess get a refund of the cess it paid on inputs such as coal?
cases.held: Yes. Section 11(2) of the Compensation Cess Act applies the refund provisions of the IGST and CGST Acts to the cess, and zero-rated supplies qualify for refund under section 16(3) of the IGST Act read with section 54. The proviso to section 11(2) did not stand in the way because no cess was payable on the exported goods, and the department had misread the two circulars in using them to refuse the refund. The rejections were set aside and the refunds allowed.
cases.effect: An exporter paying IGST on goods outside the cess net can recover the cess paid on its inputs. Compensation cess has since been reduced to nil on every good, so the ruling now matters for exports made while cess was charged on inputs — refund claims still in time and disputes about them. The Supreme Court declined to interfere.

cases.name: Shashi Ranjan Constructions Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India
cases.citation: Patna High Court, Civil Writ Jurisdiction Case No. 6700 of 2024, decided 05-05-2025 (Rajeev Ranjan Prasad and Ashok Kumar Pandey JJ.; judgment by Rajeev Ranjan Prasad J.)
cases.facts: Under a registered development agreement of 27-11-2014, a Muzaffarpur builder was to construct a building and hand 43% of the built-up area to the landowner, in exchange for 57% of the undivided share in the land. The completion certificate was issued on 20-12-2018. The State tax officer demanded about ₹4.6 crore (tax, interest and penalty) for 2018-19 on the construction supplied to the landowner. The builder argued that the land had passed to it in 2014, before GST; that handing over flats after completion was a sale of building outside GST; and that development rights were taxable only from 1 April 2019.
cases.issue: Is a builder liable to GST on the construction of the landowner's share under a development agreement signed before GST, where the flats were handed over after the completion certificate?
cases.held: Yes. The agreement did not transfer ownership of the land in 2014: the builder had no right in the property until the project was completed. What was taxed was the builder's construction service to the landowner (SAC 9954), taxable since 1 July 2017 under Notification 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate) — not the development rights, so the April 2019 changes did not matter. The builder's consideration, the development rights, had been received long before the completion certificate, so the exclusion in paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II for supplies paid for entirely after completion did not apply; Notification 4/2018 only fixes when the liability arises. Every element of the levy was present, and the writ petition was dismissed.
cases.effect: A builder pays GST on the construction of the landowner's share where the development rights came to it before completion, even under an agreement signed before GST. Follows Prahitha Construction (Telangana High Court).

cases.name: Shrinivasa Realcon Pvt. Ltd. v. Deputy Commissioner, Anti-Evasion Branch, CGST & Central Excise, Nagpur
cases.citation: Bombay High Court (Nagpur Bench), Writ Petition No. 7135 of 2024, decided 08-04-2025 (Avinash G. Gharote and Abhay J. Mantri JJ.)
cases.facts: Under a 2022 development agreement the owner of an 8,000 sq ft plot at Mouza Lendra, Nagpur appointed the petitioner as developer of a multi-storeyed building, for ₹7 crore and two apartments. The department demanded GST from the developer on reverse charge under entry 5B of Notification 13/2017-Central Tax (Rate) — services by way of transfer of development rights or FSI to a promoter — relying on a clause for a deed of declaration under the Maharashtra Apartment Ownership Act, 1970.
cases.issue: Does an ordinary development agreement, under which no TDR or FSI is bought, attract reverse charge under entry 5B?
cases.held: No. Read with 'FSI', the words 'transfer of development rights' in entry 5B mean a TDR as the Maharashtra Unified Development Control and Promotion Regulations define it — compensation in the form of FSI or development rights. They cannot be stretched to the rights a developer takes from the owner under a development agreement to build on the owner's land using its own FSI. No TDR or FSI had been bought from anyone, and a deed of declaration is not a transfer. The show cause notice and the demand order were quashed.
cases.effect: Narrow, and often overstated: reverse charge under entry 5B is not triggered by a development agreement that only lets the developer use the land's own FSI. It does not decide whether the developer's construction for the owner is taxable (Prahitha and Shashi Ranjan hold that it is) — only that entry 5B is the wrong charge.

cases.name: Tata Play Ltd. v. Union of India
cases.citation: Madras High Court, W.P. No. 17184 of 2024 and a batch of connected petitions, decided 12-06-2025 (Mohammed Shaffiq J.)
cases.facts: A large batch of taxpayers challenged section 73 notices and orders for 2017-18 to 2019-20 that were in time only because Notifications 9/2023-CT and 56/2023-CT, issued under section 168A, had extended the time limits.
cases.issue: Are Notifications 9/2023-CT and 56/2023-CT valid, and are orders passed within the extended periods time-barred?
cases.held: Both notifications are invalid. They were issued on a mistaken view of the limitation available and of the Supreme Court's order under Article 142 excluding 15-03-2020 to 28-02-2022 from limitation; they curtailed the period that order had allowed instead of extending it; they were made without examining relevant material; and 56/2023 was issued before the GST Council's recommendation, on the view of the GST Implementation Committee, which cannot take the Council's place. But the authorities keep the benefit of the Supreme Court's exclusion when counting the limits in section 73(2) and 73(10), so orders were not necessarily out of time. The matters were remanded: orders were to be treated as show cause notices, with objections within eight weeks and fresh orders after a hearing.
cases.effect: High Courts are divided — the Telangana High Court upheld Notification 56/2023 and the Gauhati High Court set it aside — and the Supreme Court has the question before it. Even if the notifications fall, the COVID-period exclusion can still keep a demand in time, so work the limitation out both ways, and keep the point alive in the reply and the appeal.

cases.name: Amazon Development Centre India Pvt. Ltd. v. Additional Commissioner of Central Tax
cases.citation: Karnataka High Court, W.P. No. 13007 of 2024, decided 17-09-2024; followed for later periods (October 2020 to September 2021) in 2025
cases.facts: Amazon Development Centre India provides pre-sale and post-sale customer support to Amazon's foreign group companies, which pay it for the service. Its claims for refund of unutilised input tax credit on these services as exports were rejected on the ground that it was an intermediary, and the appellate authority agreed (order of 04-01-2024, for October 2019 to March 2020).
cases.issue: Is customer support provided to foreign group companies an intermediary service, or an export of services?
cases.held: An export. The company supplied the support services itself, on its own account and on a principal-to-principal basis to its foreign affiliates; there was no three-party arrangement in which it arranged or facilitated a supply between two other persons, which the definition in section 2(13) and CBIC's Circular 159/15/2021 require. The services met the conditions of section 2(6), and the orders rejecting the refunds were quashed.
cases.effect: Customer-support and back-office work done for a foreign group company on your own account is not an intermediary service merely because it serves that company's customers. Relevant to supplies up to 29 March 2026 — section 13(8)(b) has since been omitted — and to refund disputes for those periods; keep the agreement and invoicing consistent with a principal-to-principal supply.

cases.name: Best Crop Science Pvt Ltd v. Principal Commissioner, CGST Commissionerate, Meerut
cases.citation: [2024] 167 taxmann.com 244 (Del), W.P.(C) No. 10980 of 2024 and connected petitions, decided 23-09-2024; Revenue SLP dismissed / judgment affirmed by the Supreme Court on 17-07-2025
cases.facts: Batch challenge to Rule 86A blocking orders, including 'negative blocking' beyond the available balance.
cases.issue: Scope of Rule 86A — can it block more than the credit available, and what reasoning is required.
cases.held: Rule 86A only allows disallowing debit of ITC available in the electronic credit ledger up to the amount believed to be fraudulently availed / ineligible; it cannot create or increase a negative balance or reach ITC yet to be credited. 'Reasons to believe' must be based on cogent material, be the officer's own, and be recorded; a block lapses automatically after one year.
cases.effect: Leading authority against 'negative blocking' and unreasoned Rule 86A orders — reinforced by the Supreme Court's dismissal of the Revenue's challenge on 17-07-2025.

cases.name: Meghmani Organochem Ltd. v. Union of India
cases.citation: Gujarat High Court, R/Special Civil Application No. 1202 of 2024, decided 14-06-2024; the Union's special leave petition (C) No. 1239 of 2025 dismissed by the Supreme Court on 22-09-2025 (J.B. Pardiwala and K.V. Viswanathan JJ.) with the question of law kept open
cases.facts: An SEZ unit at Dahej exported its goods under a letter of undertaking without paying tax, and input tax credit — including credit distributed to it by its Input Service Distributor — built up unused. Its refund claim under rule 89 was refused; the department's position was that only a supplier to an SEZ, not the SEZ unit itself, can claim such a refund.
cases.issue: Can an SEZ unit claim a refund of unutilised input tax credit accumulated on exports made under a letter of undertaking?
cases.held: Yes. Following its earlier decision in Britannia Industries (2020), the High Court held that section 54 and rule 89 do not treat an SEZ unit differently from any other registered person making zero-rated supplies without payment of tax, and that where the credit reached the unit through an ISD there is no supplier who could claim it. The Supreme Court declined to interfere 'in the peculiar facts' and given the amount involved, but kept the question of law open.
cases.effect: Supports an SEZ unit's own claim to refund of credit accumulated on exports under LUT, especially credit distributed by an ISD. Because the Supreme Court expressly left the question open, expect the department to keep contesting it elsewhere; the usual route for supplies to an SEZ remains the supplier's own refund claim.

cases.name: Prahitha Construction Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India
cases.citation: Telangana High Court, Writ Petition No. 5493 of 2020, decided 09-02-2024 (P. Sam Koshy and Laxmi Narayana Alishetty JJ.; order by P. Sam Koshy J.); SLP (C) No. 11079 of 2024 — the Supreme Court issued notice on 13-05-2024 without staying the judgment
cases.facts: A developer entered into a joint development agreement with the owners of land at Raidurg, Hyderabad, to build commercial towers on it. It asked the High Court to declare that the owners' transfer of development rights under the agreement was a sale of land outside GST (Schedule III, entry 5), and challenged Notification 4/2018-Central Tax (Rate), which fixes when tax on development rights and on the construction given in exchange falls due.
cases.issue: Is the transfer of development rights under a joint development agreement a sale of land outside GST; and is the notification valid?
cases.held: No, and yes. Read as a whole, the agreement did not pass ownership of any part of the land when it was signed: the developer acquired no right in the property until the project was completed and the completion certificate issued, and only then could it sell the area allotted to it. A joint development agreement carries two supplies — the owners' grant of development rights to the developer, and the developer's construction for the owners — and both are supplies under section 7, the construction falling within paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II. Neither is a sale of land under Schedule III. The notification, issued on the GST Council's recommendation, was upheld and the writ petition dismissed.
cases.effect: The leading ruling for the Revenue on joint development: development rights are a taxable supply, not land, and so is the developer's construction of the owner's share. The Supreme Court has issued notice on the appeal but refused a stay, recording that tax will have to be paid meanwhile; with Arham Infra Developers (a demand stayed in October 2025) the question is now before it.

cases.name: Reckitt Benckiser India Pvt Ltd v. Union of India
cases.citation: [2024] 158 taxmann.com 675 (Del) / 2024 SCC OnLine Del 615, batch of ~107 writ petitions (lead W.P.(C) 7743/2019), decided 29-01-2024
cases.facts: Batch challenge by ~107 companies (Hindustan Unilever, Nestle, Patanjali, Reckitt and others) to the constitutional validity of section 171 and anti-profiteering Rules 122, 124, 126, 127, 129, 133 and 134, and to the absence of a prescribed computation methodology.
cases.issue: Validity of the anti-profiteering framework under Articles 19(1)(g) and 300A.
cases.held: Section 171 and the rules were upheld as constitutionally valid — section 171 is a consumer-welfare / benefit-passing measure, not a price-fixing mechanism, and does not violate Article 19(1)(g) or 300A. Individual orders of the Authority remain open to challenge on merits / methodology, and the Court cautioned against arbitrary or mechanical exercise of the power.
cases.effect: Settles the vires question; SKU-level methodology and quantum disputes continue in individual appeals (now before the GST Appellate Tribunal / Principal Bench).

cases.name: Yasho Industries Ltd. v. Union of India
cases.citation: Gujarat High Court, R/Special Civil Application No. 10504 of 2023, decided 17-10-2024 (Bhargav D. Karia and D.N. Ray JJ.); the Union's special leave petition (Diary No. 17547 of 2025) dismissed by the Supreme Court on 19-05-2025 (B.V. Nagarathna and Satish Chandra Sharma JJ.)
cases.facts: The company paid the 10% pre-deposit for its first appeal — about ₹3.37 crore — by debiting its electronic credit ledger through DRC-03. The department wrote on 25-04-2023 that the pre-deposit had to be paid in cash, from the electronic cash ledger.
cases.issue: Can the pre-deposit for an appeal under section 107(6) be paid from the electronic credit ledger?
cases.held: Yes. Relying on earlier High Court rulings and on CBIC's Circular 172/04/2022-GST of 6 July 2022, which clarified that output tax payable as a consequence of any proceeding may be paid from the credit ledger, the Court held that a pre-deposit paid from the credit ledger is valid compliance with section 107(6)(b). The department's letter was quashed and the appeal directed to be heard on its merits. The Supreme Court declined to interfere, noting that the pending matters the department relied on had been brought by taxpayers, not by the department.
cases.effect: The 10% of tax in dispute can be paid from input tax credit in the credit ledger when you file a first appeal. The credit ledger can pay only output tax, so a pre-deposit on a penalty-only order still has to be paid in cash.

cases.name: Deepak Khandelwal Pvt Ltd v. Commissioner of CGST, Delhi West
cases.citation: 2023 SCC OnLine Del 4938 / [2023] 154 taxmann.com 118 (Delhi) / 2023 (78) GSTL 158 (Del), W.P.(C) 6739/2021, decided 17-08-2023; Revenue SLP dismissed by the Supreme Court (2024) and review also dismissed
cases.facts: During a search the officers seized cash and silver bars from the premises and retained them; the taxpayer sought their return.
cases.issue: Does the power to seize 'documents or books or things' in section 67(2) extend to cash and other valuables?
cases.held: 'Things' in section 67(2) takes colour from 'documents' and 'books' (ejusdem generis) and covers items useful for or relevant to the proceedings — it does not extend to cash or valuable assets that are not goods liable to confiscation. The seized currency and silver were ordered to be returned.
cases.effect: GST officers cannot seize or retain cash / jewellery / FDRs found in a search. Note a contrary view exists (M.P. High Court in Kanishka Matta), so the point is not finally settled nationally, but the Delhi HC position (SLP dismissed) is the prevailing one.

cases.name: Dharmendra M. Jani v. Union of India
cases.citation: [2023] 151 taxmann.com 271 (Bom), Writ Petition No. 2031 of 2018 — Division Bench split verdict (Ujjal Bhuyan J. holding s.13(8)(b) ultra vires, 09-06-2021; Abhay Ahuja J. holding it valid, 16-06-2021); resolved by the referral (third) judge, G.S. Kulkarni J., on 18-04-2023
cases.facts: Challenge to the constitutional validity of taxing 'intermediary' services under section 13(8)(b) read with section 8(2) of the IGST Act, where the recipient / principal is located outside India.
cases.issue: Whether section 13(8)(b) (place of supply of intermediary services in India) and section 8(2) are constitutionally valid.
cases.held: After a split verdict of the Division Bench, the referral (third) judge upheld sections 13(8)(b) and 8(2) as legal, valid and constitutional, but read them as operative only for the purposes of the IGST Act — they cannot be pressed into service to levy CGST/SGST. The double-taxation debate and contrary views of other High Courts remain unresolved, and a legislative amendment / Supreme Court reference is possible.
cases.effect: For supplies up to 29 March 2026, intermediary services with an Indian-located supplier were taxable in India and the 'export of services' route was not available. The Finance Act 2026 omitted section 13(8)(b) from 30 March 2026, so for later supplies the place of supply is the recipient's location (section 13(2)) and the ruling matters only for earlier periods and pending disputes.

cases.name: Suncraft Energy Pvt Ltd v. Assistant Commissioner, State Tax
cases.citation: 2023 (79) GSTL 156 (Cal), MAT No. 1218 of 2023, decided 02-08-2023; Revenue SLP (C) Nos. 27827-27828/2023 dismissed by the Supreme Court on 14-12-2023 (by a speaking order — relief confined to non-exceptional cases)
cases.facts: ITC was denied to the recipient because of a GSTR-2A mismatch / supplier non-payment, without any action against the supplier.
cases.issue: Can ITC be reversed in the recipient's hands for the supplier's default without first proceeding against the supplier?
cases.held: Where the recipient holds a valid invoice, has paid the supplier and the supplier was registered, ITC cannot be denied mechanically; the department must first proceed against the supplier and can recover from the recipient only in exceptional cases (missing / non-existent supplier, collusion, closure of business).
cases.effect: Gives bona fide recipients a defence against automatic section 16(2)(c) denials. The SC's dismissal of the Revenue SLP (14-12-2023) affirms it, subject to the 'exceptional cases' carve-out.

cases.name: Aggarwal Dyeing and Printing Works v. State of Gujarat
cases.citation: 2022 (61) GSTL 288 (Guj) / [2022] 137 taxmann.com 332 (Guj), decided 24-02-2022
cases.facts: Registrations were cancelled by cryptic show-cause notices and orders without reasons.
cases.issue: Validity of cancellation orders that do not disclose reasons or give a real hearing.
cases.held: Cancellation orders must be reasoned and preceded by a proper show-cause notice and hearing; cryptic orders were quashed.
cases.effect: Widely followed by High Courts to set aside mechanical GST registration cancellations.

cases.name: Munjaal Manishbhai Bhatt v. Union of India
cases.citation: Gujarat High Court, R/Special Civil Application No. 1350 of 2021 with Nos. 6840 of 2021 and 5052 of 2022, decided 06-05-2022 (J.B. Pardiwala and Nisha M. Thakore JJ.); the Union has appealed to the Supreme Court
cases.facts: The petitioner agreed to buy a 1,021 sq m plot with a bungalow of about 160 sq m to be built on it, at separate prices for the land and the construction. The developer charged 18% GST on the whole amount less the deemed one-third land deduction in paragraph 2 of Notification 11/2017-CT(Rate), which taxed far more than the construction was worth. In the connected cases the AAAR had applied the same deduction.
cases.issue: Is the mandatory one-third deduction for the value of land valid where the actual value of the land can be ascertained?
cases.held: No. Land is outside GST (Schedule III), and section 15 values a supply at its actual transaction value; a notification cannot impose a deemed land value that ignores an ascertainable actual one, and a uniform one-third for every kind of property is arbitrary and discriminatory under Article 14. Paragraph 2 was read down: the one-third deduction is not mandatory, but available at the taxable person's option where the actual value of the land or undivided share cannot be ascertained. Where the land was already developed before the agreement, no construction service arises on it. The petitioner was allowed a refund of the excess tax with 6% interest, worked out on the construction value in the agreement, and the AAAR orders were quashed.
cases.effect: Where the agreement prices the land separately, tax the construction value, not two-thirds of the total. The one-third deduction remains available by choice where the land value cannot be separated, as in most flat sales. The Union's appeal is pending in the Supreme Court, so outside Gujarat treat the point as arguable rather than settled.

cases.name: Union of India v. Bundl Technologies Pvt Ltd (Swiggy)
cases.citation: [2022] 136 taxmann.com 112 (Karnataka) / 2022 (61) GSTL 145 (Kar), W.A. No. 3660 of 2021 (Division Bench), decided 16-03-2022 (affirming the single-judge order of 14-09-2021)
cases.facts: During a DGGI investigation into alleged wrong ITC, about Rs. 27 crore was paid through DRC-03 at around 4 a.m. and the next day; no SCN was ever issued and the taxpayer had not self-ascertained any liability.
cases.issue: Can the department retain an amount 'paid' during investigation before any SCN, treating it as tax under section 74(5)?
cases.held: A payment during investigation, without a self-ascertainment under section 74(5) and without a SCN, is an involuntary deposit, not tax. The right to seek its refund is independent of the investigation and the two cannot be linked. The department was directed to consider the refund.
cases.effect: Read with CBIC Instruction 01/2022-23 — no recovery during search / investigation, and any deposit made under pressure is refundable. Section 74(5) 'self-ascertainment' must be a genuine, voluntary act by the taxpayer.

cases.name: Vallabh Textiles v. Senior Intelligence Officer
cases.citation: 2022 SCC OnLine Del 4508 / [2023] 146 taxmann.com 421 (Delhi) / 2023 (68) GSTL 3 (Del), W.P.(C) 9834/2022, decided 20-12-2022
cases.facts: Around Rs. 1.8 crore was 'deposited' by the taxpayer through DRC-03 during and immediately after an overnight search, allegedly under pressure.
cases.issue: Is tax collected during a search, without the safeguards of CBIC Instruction 01/2022-23, voluntary?
cases.held: Collection of tax during search hours, without giving the taxpayer time to reflect or consult, and without following Instruction 01/2022-23 (which bars recovery during search and requires any payment to be genuinely voluntary), is not a voluntary payment. The amount was ordered to be refunded with interest at 6%.
cases.effect: You are not obliged to pay anything during a search. If pressured, note it in the panchnama, pay nothing, and claim a refund of any coerced DRC-03.

cases.name: D.Y. Beathel Enterprises v. State Tax Officer
cases.facts: ITC was recovered from the recipient where the supplier had collected but not paid the tax; the supplier was not examined.
cases.issue: Recovery from the recipient without joining / examining the defaulting supplier.
cases.held: The recovery was set aside; the department must examine and proceed against the supplier before recovering from the recipient.
cases.effect: Supplier must be joined before ITC is recovered from a bona fide recipient.

cases.name: Greenwood Owners Association v. Union of India
cases.citation: Madras High Court, W.P. Nos. 5518 & 1555 of 2020 and 27100 & 30004 of 2019, decided 01-07-2021 (Dr. Anita Sumanth J.); on the Revenue's writ appeal a Division Bench is reported to have stayed the judgment (07-10-2021)
cases.facts: Associations of apartment owners in Chennai challenged the Tamil Nadu AAR's ruling, and CBIC Circular 109/28/2019-GST, that where a member's monthly contribution to a resident welfare association exceeds ₹7,500, GST is payable on the whole contribution and not just the excess.
cases.issue: Is the whole contribution taxable once it exceeds ₹7,500 a month per member, or only the part above ₹7,500?
cases.held: Only the part above ₹7,500. Entry 77(c) of Notification 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate) exempts contributions 'up to an amount of' ₹7,500 a month per member; 'up to' marks a ceiling, so contributions up to it are exempt and only the excess is taxed. Where the Government meant an exemption to be lost entirely once a limit is crossed, it said so in terms — as in the entry for artists' performances — and exemption notifications are read strictly both ways. The AAR's ruling and the circular, on this point, were quashed.
cases.effect: Only the excess over ₹7,500 is taxable — but the ruling was stayed on appeal, so CBIC's position (the whole contribution is taxable once over ₹7,500) is what officers apply pending the appeal. An association with turnover up to ₹20 lakh need not register at all.

cases.name: Mahadeo Construction Co. v. Union of India
cases.citation: 2020 (34) GSTL 15 (Jhar) / [2020] 116 taxmann.com 262 (Jharkhand), W.P.(T) No. 3517 of 2019, decided 21-04-2020
cases.facts: Interest under section 50 was demanded and recovery initiated for a delay in filing GSTR-3B, without any adjudication, on the footing that it was an 'admitted' liability.
cases.issue: Can interest under section 50 be recovered by coercive action without first adjudicating the amount?
cases.held: Interest is compensatory and arises automatically, but where the taxpayer disputes the period of delay or the quantum (e.g. the ITC-vs-cash split, or whether the return was actually late), that dispute must be decided through a proper proceeding under section 73 / 74 with a hearing. Interest is not 'self-assessed tax' that can be recovered under section 79 without adjudication.
cases.effect: A disputed section 50 interest demand needs a SCN and an order before the department can attach bank accounts or issue DRC-13. Contest the computation at the SCN stage.

cases.name: Refex Industries Ltd v. Assistant Commissioner
cases.facts: Interest demanded on the gross output tax for a late GSTR-3B where ITC was available.
cases.issue: Whether interest is on gross tax or on the net cash liability.
cases.held: Interest is payable only on the cash component; the proviso to section 50(1) is clarificatory and retrospective.
cases.effect: Anchored the 'interest on net cash' position later confirmed by the retrospective amendment.

cases.name: Adfert Technologies Pvt Ltd v. Union of India
cases.citation: 2019 SCC OnLine P&H 5701 / [2019] 111 taxmann.com 27 (P&H) / 2020 (32) GSTL 726 (P&H), CWP No. 30949 of 2018, decided 04-11-2019; Revenue SLP dismissed by the Supreme Court on 28-02-2020, [2020] 115 taxmann.com 249 (SC)
cases.facts: Taxpayers could not carry forward accumulated CENVAT / VAT credit because TRAN-1 could not be filed or revised in time due to portal glitches.
cases.issue: Can unutilised transitional credit be denied for a technical failure to meet the TRAN-1 deadline?
cases.held: Unutilised input tax credit earned under the earlier laws is a vested right and 'property' under Article 300A; it cannot be taken away for a procedural or technical lapse where the taxpayer was otherwise entitled. The department was directed to permit filing / correction of TRAN-1.
cases.effect: The leading pre-Filco authority that transitional credit is a substantive right, not a concession that lapses with a form deadline. The SC's dismissal of the Revenue SLP (28-02-2020) affirms it.

cases.name: Amit Cotton Industries v. Principal Commissioner of Customs
cases.citation: Gujarat High Court, R/Special Civil Application No. 20126 of 2018, decided 27-06-2019 (J.B. Pardiwala & A.C. Rao, JJ.); reported at 2019 (29) GSTL 200 (Guj) / [2019] 107 taxmann.com 167 (Gujarat)
cases.facts: A cotton ginning mill exported cotton bales to Bangladesh in July 2017 on payment of IGST (about 19.05 lakh over three shipping bills) and also claimed duty drawback at the higher composite rate. Customs withheld the IGST-paid export refund, relying on the declaration required for higher drawback and on CBIC Circular 37/2018-Customs (9-10-2018), under which an exporter who claims the higher drawback rate is treated as having relinquished the IGST-refund claim. The exporter then repaid the differential drawback with interest and pressed for the refund; Customs still declined, saying the process is fully system-driven with no way to handle such a claim.
cases.issue: Whether an IGST-paid export refund can be withheld merely because the exporter initially claimed drawback at the higher rate, relying on CBIC Circular 37/2018-Customs, when neither ground for withholding under Rule 96(4) of the CGST Rules is present.
cases.held: The refund could not be withheld. Rule 96 creates a deeming fiction that the shipping bill is the refund application, and Rule 96(4) makes it 'abundantly clear' that a refund can be withheld only in the two situations in sub-clauses (a) and (b) — a withholding request from the jurisdictional Commissioner under section 54(10)/(11), or a Customs finding that the goods were exported in violation of the Customs Act — and the department fairly conceded neither applied. Circular 37/2018-Customs 'cannot be said to have any legal force' and 'cannot run contrary to the statutory rules, more particularly, Rule 96'; a circular contrary to statute 'has really no existence in law' (following Ratan Melting & Wire Industries and J.K. Lakshmi Cement, SC). The court also noted the circular post-dates the export (9-10-2018 vs 27-7-2017) and deals with drawback, not the IGST refund. 'Rule 96 of the Rules, 2017, is very clear.'
cases.effect: The writ was allowed and Customs directed to sanction the IGST refund with 7% simple interest from the date of the shipping bills to actual refund. Widely followed by High Courts for the proposition that Rule 96(4) is an exhaustive list of the grounds to withhold an IGST-paid export refund and a circular cannot add to it. The list itself has since grown: clause (c) — verification of the exporter's credentials, including ITC availed, on data analysis and risk parameters — came in by Notification 14/2022-CT, so there are now three grounds. Separately, Rule 96(10) (a different bar, on concessional duty-free imports) was omitted with effect from 8 October 2024.

cases.name: Synergy Fertichem Pvt Ltd v. State of Gujarat
cases.citation: 2020 (33) GSTL 3 (Guj) / [2019] 111 taxmann.com 313 (Guj), decided 23-12-2019
cases.facts: Confiscation proceedings initiated straight after detention for an e-way bill lapse.
cases.issue: When can section 130 confiscation be invoked as against section 129 detention?
cases.held: Section 130 requires an independent finding of intent to evade tax; it cannot be invoked mechanically on the back of a section 129 detention.
cases.effect: The reference point for challenging premature confiscation; reinforced by the 2022 de-linking amendment.

cases.name: A-1 Cuisines Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India
cases.citation: Bombay High Court (Nagpur Bench), Writ Petition No. 8034 of 2018, decided 28-11-2018 (P.N. Deshmukh and Swapna Joshi JJ.; oral judgment by P.N. Deshmukh J.)
cases.facts: The petitioner wanted to open a shop in the domestic security hold area of Nagpur airport, selling cosmetics and perfumes to passengers flying to an international hub to leave India on a connecting flight. It sought a direction that it could sell without GST and claim refund of input taxes, like the duty-free shops in international terminals.
cases.issue: Does the duty-free treatment of shops beyond the customs frontier extend to a shop in a domestic departure area that sells to passengers who will leave India on a connecting flight?
cases.held: No. Following Hotel Ashoka, sales at duty-free shops in the arrival or departure halls of international airports, after immigration, take place beyond the customs frontiers — outside India — and are non-taxable supplies in non-taxable territory. That does not extend to a shop at a domestic airport or in a domestic security hold area, before immigration: the sale takes place in India, a domestic passenger may or may not go abroad, and customs cannot check that the goods leave the country. The petition was dismissed.
cases.effect: GST applies to sales in domestic departure areas, even to passengers holding onward international boarding passes. Whether indirect tax reaches duty-free shops in the international areas is a separate question, open again since the Supreme Court recalled its 2023 Flemingo order.

cases.name: Builders Association of Navi Mumbai v. Union of India
cases.citation: Bombay High Court, Writ Petition No. 12194 of 2017, decided 28-03-2018 (S.C. Dharmadhikari and Prakash D. Naik JJ.); special leave petition (C) No. 23068 of 2018 dismissed by the Supreme Court on 09-11-2022 (Sanjiv Khanna and J.K. Maheshwari JJ.), leaving two questions open
cases.facts: CIDCO, the statutory new-town development authority for Navi Mumbai, allots plots to builders on 60-year leases for a one-time lease premium plus annual rent, and collected 18% GST on the premium. A builders' association argued that such a lease by a statutory authority is in substance a sale of land, outside GST, and that the premium is a capital payment.
cases.issue: Is GST payable on the one-time premium for a long lease of land granted by a statutory development authority?
cases.held: Yes. Section 7(1)(a) covers every form of supply — lease included — made for a consideration in the course or furtherance of business, and Schedule II paragraph 2(a) treats any lease of land as a supply of services. CIDCO is a person that disposes of land by lease for a consideration, whatever the payment is called, and no notification under section 7(2) takes its activity out of supply. The demand was lawful. The Supreme Court saw no reason to differ, but said it had not examined the exemption under Notification 12/2017-CT(Rate) or the scope of 'licence to occupy land' in paragraph 2(a) of Schedule II, and left both open.
cases.effect: A lease premium, even for a 60-year lease from a statutory authority, is consideration for a service, not the price of land. Check whether entry 41 of Notification 12/2017-CT(Rate) — the upfront amount for a lease of 30 years or more of industrial plots by State industrial development corporations and similar government entities — applies; the Supreme Court left the exemption question open, and the plots in this case were residential-cum-commercial.
